children.text: This park on the summit of Mount Sungay, the highest point in Cavite, turned the site of the "Palace in the Sky," left unfinished in the Marcos era, into a public park. From viewing decks about 709m above sea level you look down on Taal Lake, Volcano Island, and Tagaytay Ridge in every direction, and an hour or so is enough to see it all.
People's Park in the Sky is a viewpoint park on the summit of Mount Sungay (Mount Gonzales), at the eastern end of Tagaytay City. The summit stands about

above sea level, the highest point in Cavite Province, and looks down on Taal Lake and Volcano Island in the middle of the lake from a level well above the cafes and parks that line Tagaytay Ridge. A walk around the summit opens up views in every direction, not only of the lake to the south but also the Cavite plains to the north and the mountain ranges toward Laguna to the east, which is why locals know it as the highest viewpoint in Tagaytay. "Sungay" means "horn" in Tagalog, a name that came from the once-pointed shape of the old peak.
The site has an unusual history. Around

, under the direction of Imelda Marcos, the Marcos government began building a presidential retreat and state guesthouse on this peak, the "Palace in the Sky," and rushed the work ahead of a visit by U.S. President Reagan planned for
November 1983
. After Senator Ninoy Aquino was assassinated that August, the visit was canceled, construction stopped, and only the concrete frame was left. The peak, originally about
high, was cut down to its present height during construction. It was opened to the public after the People Power Revolution of

, and in the mid-1990s, on the orders of President Ramos, Tagaytay City restored it and gave it its current name, the "People's Park." The project also won a Galing Pook Award, which honors outstanding local governance programs in the Philippines, in

Today the park is run directly by Tagaytay City. The unfinished main building with telecom towers rising above it, the white Doppler weather radar dome of the Philippine weather agency (PAGASA), and the shrine chapel of Our Lady, Mother of Fair Love, set on the hillside, occupy the summit, surrounded by viewing railings, walking paths, and fruit and souvenir stalls. Rather than a polished attraction, it is a place where frozen-in-time concrete ruins meet a wide-open sky, which also gives it meaning as a site that shows how the extravagance of one era became a public retreat.
1–1.5 hours
is enough for a visit. It lies about
8.5km

east of the Rotonda in the city center, so it is usually combined with other Tagaytay sights for a half-day plan. It suits travelers who want to see the volcano views from the ridge from even higher up, those who like places with a story, and families who want a day trip from Manila for some cool air. For general travel information on the area, see the
Tagaytay
entry as well.

Walking along the summit railing, you take in Taal Lake and Volcano Island to the south, Tagaytay Ridge and lakeside towns to the west, and the Cavite plains to the north. On very clear days you can see as far as Laguna Lake, Manila Bay, Mount Makiling, and Mount Banahaw.

blocks.title: Looking down on Taal Lake and Volcano Island

children.text: Volcano Island lying low in the middle of the lake, the lakeside towns, and the fish pens on the water all come into view at once. On mornings when clouds hang low, a sea of clouds sometimes drifts below the ridge, and you may find yourself leaning on the deck railing and gazing for a long time.

blocks.title: The unfinished "Palace in the Sky" main building

children.text: A concrete building left unfinished in the Marcos era still stands with its columns and steel frame exposed. The rusty roofs and moss-covered walls remain as they were, making it a good place to take photos while thinking about the story of that era. Do not enter areas that have been roped off.

blocks.title: Shrine chapel of Our Lady, Mother of Fair Love

children.text: A white chapel and a statue of the Virgin Mary stand on a retaining wall along the road up to the summit. According to the plaque, the shrine was dedicated on
February 14, 2003
, and on weekends you often see local families lighting candles and praying. The steps in front of the chapel are also a good viewing spot.

The white ball-shaped structure on the summit is the Doppler weather radar of the Philippine weather agency. It can be seen from as far away as Picnic Grove and the ridge road, serving as a landmark for spotting Mount Sungay. The facility is closed to the public.

blocks.title: Browsing the stalls at the entrance plaza

children.text: Fruit and snack stalls and souvenir shops gather around the entrance plaza and along the uphill road. It is a nice place to rest with a warm drink or a light snack in the cool breeze, and the lively weekend atmosphere, with local families out for the day, is part of the fun.
Take a bus bound for Tagaytay or Nasugbu from PITX in Manila. On weekends, it is better to set off even earlier.
Get off near Olivarez or the Rotonda and switch to a jeepney or tricycle bound for People's Park.
Buy your entrance ticket and ride the shuttle jeepney up to the summit.
Walk a full circle around the 360-degree viewing deck and photograph Taal Lake and Volcano Island. This is the clearest time, before the clouds rise.
Take a slow look around the main building of the unfinished Palace in the Sky and the radar dome.
Stop by the shrine chapel of Our Lady, Mother of Fair Love, then walk down the hill road.
Take a break at the entrance plaza stalls, then return to town by jeepney or the tricycle you arranged in advance.
Finish with an early bulalo lunch at the restaurants along the ridge.
Start with the morning views at People's Park in the Sky.
Move to Picnic Grove, about 10 minutes away by car, and walk its viewing deck and forest trail.
Have a bulalo lunch at the Mahogany Market restaurant row.
Ride the Ferris wheel at Sky Ranch or relax at a ridge-top cafe.
Buy gifts such as buko pie and head back to Manila.
The top of Mount Sungay is often wrapped in clouds from late morning. Seeing the views first thing in the morning and filling the afternoon with sights in town is the best order.
Take a bus bound for Tagaytay, Nasugbu, or Mendez from PITX in Parañaque or a terminal in the Pasay area of Manila. The trip takes about
1.5–3 hours
depending on traffic, and the fare is about
Buses do not go to the park itself. Get off at Olivarez or the Rotonda in the city center and transfer to a jeepney or tricycle.
Jeepneys with a "People's Park" sign run from around Olivarez and the market area. The fare is about
, and it takes
20–30 minutes
to reach the entrance below the summit.
Hiring a tricycle costs about
one way. Since it can be hard to find a ride back from the park, negotiate in advance for the driver to wait and then take you on to your next stop.
From Manila, exit SLEX at Santa Rosa and take the Santa Rosa–Tagaytay Road, or use CALAX to drive up to Tagaytay. It takes about
1.5–2.5 hours
From the Rotonda, follow the road east toward Calamba (Tagaytay–Calamba Road) to reach the park entrance. If you are coming from Calamba in Laguna, you can drive straight up this road.
Parking is
for a car, and the entrance parking lot fills up quickly on weekend mornings.

In Tagaytay,
November–May
is the dry season and
June–October
is the rainy season. Since the views are everything here,
November–March

, with clear skies and cool breezes, is the best time. The summit, at over 700m, is windier and cooler than even the ridge in town, so you will need a light jacket in the mornings at this time of year. In
April–May
, even on sunny days, haze often blurs the distant mountains.
Early morning is the clearest time of day. The summit is often inside the clouds after

, so try to arrive before 9 if you can. In the rainy season there are days when the summit is shrouded in fog all day and the lake cannot be seen at all, and the park may close when a typhoon approaches. On the other hand, you may catch the moment the clouds part and Volcano Island appears above a sea of clouds. On weekends, public holidays, and the Holy Week break, crowds of day-trippers make the shuttle and parking lot busy.

There is no lodging in the park, so you stay in Tagaytay. To catch the early-morning views, places on the Calamba road side to the east, near Picnic Grove, mean a shorter trip. If you are getting around by public transportation, the Rotonda and Olivarez area, close to bus stops and malls, is convenient. Mid-range hotels with lake-view rooms cost about
a night, and simple guesthouses about
; book early for weekends and holidays.

The summit stalls offer only fruit, light snacks, and drinks, so have proper meals in town. The signature dish of cool Tagaytay is bulalo, a soup of beef shank and bone marrow simmered for hours, and the restaurant row around Mahogany Market to the west is famous as bulalo street. It takes
30–40 minutes

by car from the park to Mahogany Market. The view cafes along the ridge are good places to spend the afternoon with coffee and buko pie, and fried tawilis, a freshwater fish found only in Taal Lake, is another local specialty.
Opening hours are generally given as
, but they can change with the weather and events, so check on site.
The views are best in the morning. Plan to be standing on the summit before
, before the clouds rise.
The entrance fee, shuttle, and stalls are all cash only. Bring plenty of small bills such as ₱20 and ₱50, and note that senior and PWD discounts apply only when you show ID.
The climb is steep, so riding the shuttle up and walking down is easier on your knees. Wear sneakers with firm soles.
The summit is windy and cooler than town. Bring a windbreaker or a thin long-sleeved top, and wear a hat with a strap so it does not blow away.
If you came by tricycle, agree on a waiting time with the driver. Empty vehicles are rare in front of the park, and Grab is hard to get.
The shuttle line and parking lot get crowded on weekend and holiday mornings. For a relaxed visit, weekday mornings are best.
Leashed pets are said to be allowed, but alcohol is prohibited. Rules may change, so follow the notices at the entrance.
Combining the park with Picnic Grove, on the same Calamba road side, keeps travel short. Sky Ranch and Mahogany Market to the west are
30–40 minutes
away by car, so plan your route from east to west.
Taal Volcano, which the park overlooks, is an active volcano. As of
October 2026

, the alert level of the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) is 1, but the institute stresses that Level 1 does not mean the risk of eruption has passed. Volcano Island is a permanent danger zone where landing is prohibited. The park may close if the alert level rises or a volcanic gas warning is issued, so check the latest advisories before you set out.
Many parts of the unfinished main building and older facilities are run-down, with rusty roofs and cracked walls. Do not enter roped-off areas or the slopes beyond the railings.
The climb from the entrance to the summit is steep and slippery after rain. On foggy days visibility is poor, so walk along the edge of the road used by cars and shuttles.
The summit is the highest point around, so there is a risk of lightning strikes during thunderstorms. Head down right away if you see lightning.
Heavy rain in the rainy season brings a risk of landslides on the slopes around Mount Sungay. Postpone your visit on days with typhoon or heavy rain warnings.
Keep an eye on your phone and bag in the weekend crowds, and do not stand on the railings to take photos.
